Four-Cycle Engine Theory Section 2: Four-Cycle Engine Theory Introduction Four events must occur in the correct sequence and at the correct time for the engine to run correctly. These events are (A) intake, (B) compression, (C) ignition and power, and (D) exhaust. (A) Intake (C) Power 001684 The piston is traveling from top dead center (TDC) to bottom dead center (BDC). The cam has opened the intake valve. The piston's downward movement in the cylinder creates a partial vacuum in the cylinder. Air at atmospheric pressure is drawn into the cylinder through the carburetor and is mixed with fuel in the carburetor. The fuel-air mixture flows through the open intake valve into the cylinder. The intake stroke is complete when the piston reaches BDC. (B) Compression 001686 Combustion is already in progress when the piston reaches TDC. The intake and exhaust valves remain closed as expanding gases of combustion force the piston downward. (D) Exhaust 001687 The exhaust stroke begins when the piston has reached BDC and has started its upward movement. The intake valve is closed, and the exhaust valve is open to let gases escape. 001685 As the piston reaches BDC, both the intake and exhaust valves are closed. The piston moves upward toward TDC and the fuel-air mixture is compressed. Ignition occurs just before the piston reaches TDC. Generac 426/460 Engine Service Manual 9

Troubleshooting Most complaints concerning engine operation can be classified as one or a combination of the following: • Will not start • Hard starting • Lack of power • Runs rough • Vibration • Overheating • High oil consumption NOTE: What appears to be an engine malfunction may be a fault of the powered equipment, rather than the engine. If equipment is suspect, see equipment affecting engine operation. Systematic Inspection If engine will not start and the cause of malfunction is not readily apparent, perform a systematic inspection in the following order: 1. Fuel 2. Ignition 3. Compression This inspection, performed in a systematic manner, can usually be done in a matter of minutes. It is the quickest and surest method of determining the cause of failure. The basic inspection procedure is the same for all engine models. Any variation, by model, will be shown under the subject heading. Checking Fuel • Are the fuel tanks full? • Is the fuel stale? • Is the fuel tank vent open? • Is the fuel shutoff valve open? Checking Ignition See Ignition. Checking Compression Proceed as follows to check engine compression using master compression gauge kit (Generac part number GN04001): 1. Remove spark plug. 2. Insert an automotive type compression gauge into spark plug hole. 3. Crank engine until there is no further increase in pressure. The highest reading obtained is the engine compression pressure. • 426/460cc engines: Minimum 55 psi (379 kPa) 12 Generac 426/460 Engine Service Manual

This minimum reading may appear low. This is due to the engine being equipped with a compression release mechanism to minimize starting effort. Actual running compression will be much higher (see Compression Release). If compression is poor, look for one or more of the following causes: • Loose cylinder head bolts • Failed cylinder head gasket • Burned / worn valves or valve seats • Insufficient valve clearance • Warped cylinder head • Warped valve stem or worn valve guides • Worn or broken piston ring(s) • Worn or damaged cylinder bore • Broken connecting rod Cylinder Leakdown Test A cylinder leakdown tester (Generac P/N 0F77000SRV) may be used to test the sealing capability of compression components of the cylinder at TDC, and quickly identify the problem component. A cylinder leakdown test will assist in troubleshooting leaking valves or rings. See Figure 3-6. There are two gauges on the tester. One measures incoming air pressure, and the other measures percent of cylinder leakage. Proceed as follows to perform a cylinder leakdown test: 1. Align piston at TDC. 2. Install cylinder leakdown tester in spark plug hole. 3. Pressurize cylinder to 90 psi (621 kPa). 4. Observe cylinder leakage and identify location of air leak. NOTE: If leaking into intake or exhaust port, check valve clearance, valve face, and seat condition. General Information Generac 426/460 Engine Service Manual 13

Mechanical Governor (If Equipped) Section 5: Mechanical Governor (If Equipped) Governor Operation See Figure 5-1. The governor spring (A) tends to pull governor shaft (B), governor lever (C), and governor rod (D) toward the “Increase RPM” direction (E). A DC B J G K E Governor Internal Parts See Figure 5-2. The governor gear shaft (A) is pressed into a bore in the engine crankcase cover. Internal governor components include a thrust washer (B), governor gear assembly (C), snap ring (D), governor spool (E), and governor arm (H). A lock pin and washer (F, G) retain the governor arm in the crankcase cover. A B C D F H 001740 A Governor spring F Flyweight B Governor shaft G Centrifugal force C Governor lever H Governor spool D Governor rod J Governor gear E Increase RPM K Decrease RPM Figure 5-1. Governor Operating Diagram As engine speed increases, centripetal force acts on flyweight (F). When flyweight centrifugal force (G) exceeds governor spring force, governor spool (H) is moved axially by flyweight force. This causes governor gear (J) to rotate, which then moves governor lever and governor rod toward the “Decrease RPM” direction (K). As engine speed decreases, a point is reached where governor spring force is greater than flyweight centrifugal force. Governor spring force then moves governor lever and governor rod toward “Increase RPM.” Governor action consists of a series of small rpm overshoots and undershoots, as governor spring force increases rpm and flyweight centripetal force decreases rpm. The point at which spring tension and flyweight force are equal is the governed speed of the engine. Internal Governor Parts The governor gear assembly houses governor flyweights. Flyweight movement causes governor spool to move axially. Recoil Starter (If Equipped) Section 7: Recoil Starter (If Equipped) Overview The recoil starter used on portable equipment engines is a manual starter that uses a spring to rewind the starter rope after it has been pulled. Pulling the rope winds a clock-type spiral spring in the starter housing. When the rope is released, the spring unwinds and causes the rope to wind around the pulley. When the rope is pulled outward and away from the engine, spring-loaded “starter dogs” engage the pulley, and the engine is cranked. When the rope is allowed to return, the starter dogs disengage from the pulley. Electric Starter (If Equipped) Section 8: Electric Starter (If Equipped) Introduction The Generac 426/460cc engine may be equipped with a 12 volt DC electric cranking system. Such a system converts electrical energy from a battery into mechanical energy at the starter motor. The starter motor then turns the engine over. NOTE: Cranking systems discussed in this manual are typical systems. Actual cranking system used in specific applications may differ. See wiring diagram and/or electrical schematic in owner's manual for specific applications. Starter Motor Operating Principles See Figure 8-1. Closing the circuit to the starter motor (A) allows battery current to flow through a commutator, to the loops of wire in the armature, and back to the battery. The interaction of the magnetic fields causes the armature to revolve. B A 009677 Figure 8-1. Electric Starter The armature rotates at a relatively high speed to provide sufficient torque to crank the engine. The required engine cranking speed is relatively slow, so the starter motor is equipped with a small drive pinion that meshes with the teeth of a flywheel ring gear (B) to crank engine. The large ring gear and small starter pinion gear results in a gear reduction that can vary in ratio up to 19-to-1. This reduction allows the starter to rotate at high speeds while cranking the engine at low speeds. Speed increases quickly when the engine starts. For example, if the engine reaches 100 rpm and starter pinion remains meshed with ring gear, the starter armature would spin at about 1,900 rpm (19-to-1 ratio). To prevent damage to the armature, a "Bendix" drive mechanism is used to disengage starter pinion from the ring gear when the engine has started. Bendix Drive The armature starts to rotate when field coils of the starter drive are energized. A loose fitting sleeve inside the pinion gear rotates with the armature. This sleeve has large spiral threads on its surface matching the pinion gear’s internal threads. The sleeve rotates with the armature, and pinion gear rotates on the threads to move outward on the sleeve. Outward movement of the pinion gear causes the pinion gear to mesh with the flywheel ring gear. As soon as the pinion gear engages a stop on the sleeve, the pinion gear rotates the ring gear and engine. The engine rotates faster than the armature on startup. This causes the pinion to spin back on the spiral threads of the sleeve and out of engagement with the ring gear. Starter Motor Repair A faulty starter motor should be removed and replaced. Starter motor disassembly and repair is not cost-effective. Removing the Starter Motor WARNING Accidental start-up. Disconnect negative battery terminal before servicing to prevent accidental engine rotation. Failure to do so could result in death or serious injury. (000148a) To remove starter motor from engine, loosen and disconnect the starter wire, then remove the two hex head screws holding the starter in place. Installing the Starter Motor Reverse previous steps to install starter motor. Testing the Starter Motor Checking the Pinion The pinion gear should rise and engage the ring gear when the starter motor is activated. If the pinion gear does not rise normally, inspect the large spiral threads of the sleeve and pinion for binding or sticking. Section 9: Lubrication System Lubrication System Overview The engine lubrication system serves to (a) reduce friction between moving parts, (b) cool the engine, and (c) establish a negative pressure in the crankcase to prevent oil seal leakage. Major components include the following: • Oil pickup assembly • Oil pump • Crankshaft oil seals • Pressure relief valve • Breather assembly • Crankcase cover • Low Oil Pressure Switch Optional Systems In addition to the major components listed above, some engines may be equipped with an optional oil filter. Oil Flow See Figure 9-1. An oil pickup screen extends into the crankcase. The oil pump draws crankcase oil through the oil pickup screen and delivers it to areas requiring lubrication. 5 4 2 3 1 6 004040 Figure 9-1. Lubrication System Diagram 1. If equipped, oil will pass through an oil filter and through a cored passage in the crankcase cover. 2. The cored passage in the crankcase cover allows oil to reach the oil pump and one camshaft bearing surface. Oil flows through the cored passage in the cover and also flows to one crankshaft bearing. 3. Oil flows through the hollow camshaft to lubricate the camshaft bearing at the opposite end of the camshaft. 4. Oil flows through the crankshaft and to the crank throw to lubricate the rod bearing. 5. If oil pressure exceeds 40 psi (276 kPa), the oil pressure relief valve opens. Oil Pickup Assembly See Figure 9-2. The oil pickup assembly consists of a cylindrical plastic tube with a screen. Two o-ring seals are installed in grooves at one end of the cylinder. The pickup slides into a bore of the oil filter pad in the crankcase cover and extends into the interior of the crankcase. Once installed in the crankcase cover bore, the pickup is retained by either of the following methods: Figure 9-2. Section 13: Troubleshooting Troubleshooting Problem Solving Introduction Problems affecting engine operation may be classified as one of, or a combination of two or more of the following: • Engine will not start • Engine starts with difficulty • Engine lacks power • Engine vibrates • Engine overheats • Engine burns oil In many cases, the cause of a problem will be readily apparent. If this is not the case, inspect the fuel system, ignition system, and engine compression. These inspections can be performed quickly and are the best methods of finding the cause of a failure. They may also provide early detection of future failures. Checking Fuel System NOTE: If using in home standby product, use generator diagnostic manual for troubleshooting fuel system. Verify fuel tank has been correctly filled with the correct fuel. Verify fuel shutoff valve is open, if equipped, and fuel is flowing through the fuel line and to the carburetor. Adjust carburetor as needed. Verify choke closes completely. Remove and inspect spark plug if engine still does not start. If plug is WET, look for the following: • Overchoking • Dirty air cleaner • Excessively rich fuel-air mixture • Water in fuel • Fuel leaking past the carburetor float needle If plug is DRY, look for the following: • Carburetor mounting gasket leaks • Dirt or gum in carburetor or fuel line • Carburetor float needle stuck closed • Inoperative fuel pump (if equipped) • Clogged fuel filter (if equipped) Checking Ignition System See Ignition. Checking Compression Proceed as follows to check engine compression: 1. Remove spark plug. 2. Insert an automotive type compression gauge into spark plug hole. 3. Crank engine until there is no further increase in pressure. The highest reading obtained is the engine compression pressure. If compression is poor, inspect for one or more of the following causes: • Loose cylinder head bolts • Failed cylinder head gasket • Burned valves or valve seats • Insufficient valve clearance • Warped cylinder head • Warped valve stem • Worn or broken piston ring(s) • Worn or damaged cylinder bore • Broken connecting rod • Worn valve seats or valves • Worn valve guides Generac 426/460 Engine Service Manual 49
